title: What is actually implemented
deck: A capability is more than a schema field or an endpoint name.

blocks.text: You have a working user-service foundation: local authentication, signed access tokens, rotating refresh sessions, account profiles, media, role-protected administration, and Discord login. The new linking routes now let an authenticated user add Discord as a login method. The testing frontend exercises part of this surface.

blocks.text: Read the evidence precisely. Source review describes the working tree, including your uncommitted frontend changes. Automated checks verify selected behaviors. A passing build does not prove a real Discord browser handshake works. Deferred architecture, such as MQ notifications, is a plan rather than deployed functionality.

blocks.text: Which features have database structure but no usable workflow? Two-factor authentication, recovery codes and online status are good places to start. What would you need to observe before calling each one complete?

title: The whole system at a glance

blocks.caption: The frontend talks to HTTP endpoints. Prisma translates database operations; it is not a separate network service.

blocks.text: AuthModule answers who can sign in and how application credentials are issued or revoked. AccountsModule owns profile data and images. SuperadminModule owns privileged user-management operations. Each module registers the providers and controllers Nest needs to construct.

PrismaService is shared through a global module and connects using the PostgreSQL settings. ConfigService is also available globally. AuthModule configures JwtService and exports the access-token guard and JWT module so other modules can authenticate requests without duplicating token setup.

blocks.caption: Discord's token and our access token belong to different systems and have different audiences.

blocks.text: What other containers can use

Chat or game can verify our RS256 access-token signature with the public key, and can fetch public profiles or image URLs over HTTP. They do not need our private key. Your intended MQ model would maintain their own local user projections, but event publishing and consumers are not implemented here.

blocks.text: For each arrow, what crosses the boundary: a password, a JWT, a provider code, a user ID, or image bytes? Which component is allowed to decide whether a user is SUPERADMIN?

title: What Nest does with a request

blocks.caption: Then the controller calls a service, which may query Prisma. Response interceptors and exception handling complete the HTTP response.

blocks.text: A controller decorator such as @Get('me') maps a method to a route under its controller prefix. @Req() supplies the request; @Body() supplies parsed input; @Param() supplies route parameters. The method usually delegates the actual decision to a service.

For GET /accounts/me, AccessTokenGuard verifies the Bearer token and attaches request.user.sub. The controller passes that ID to AccountsService.getMe(). Prisma selects the private account fields. Nest serializes the returned object as JSON. The user ID comes from the verified token, never a caller-supplied profile ID.
Validation and error handling

The global ValidationPipe transforms DTO input, permits declared validation fields, and rejects extra fields. Guards run before pipes, so an unauthenticated request can return 401 before an invalid body is examined. The image upload interceptor also runs before the controller and enforces multipart limits.

Throwing BadRequestException, UnauthorizedException, ForbiddenException, NotFoundException or ConflictException lets Nest produce the corresponding HTTP response. You do not need a repeated controller try/catch for each one. Unexpected programming or database errors are different: an uncaught failure becomes a server error, not automatically a meaningful 409.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: Predict the response to PATCH /accounts/me with no token and {role:'SUPERADMIN'}. Then add a valid token and try the same body. Why do the two requests fail at different layers?

A constructor such as constructor(private readonly jwt: JwtService) is a dependency request. Nest resolves the registered JwtService and passes it into the class. Your service does not read key files or manually construct a new JWT library on every request.

This is a schematic of the actual factory. registerAsync lets configuration depend on injected providers; the factory itself does not have to contain await. Nest calls it during setup and uses its returned options to construct JwtService. Later, signAsync() and verifyAsync() use those options.

ConfigModule.forRoot() loads configuration for Nest. The JWT factory reads the private/public PEM values, replaces literal backslash-n sequences with line breaks, parses the keys, requires an RSA pair of at least 2048 bits, and checks that the public key matches the private key. A bad pair fails startup early.

Not that it is unique, uncompromised or hard to guess.

blocks.text: A character count is not a byte count. Twenty four-byte emoji can fit the character limit while exceeding bcrypt's 72-byte input limit. The separate byte check prevents accepting inputs whose trailing bytes bcrypt would ignore. Login checks an input byte bound but does not reapply all new-password rules to existing credentials.

The service explicitly chooses fields for the database write. This remains a useful second boundary even if a caller bypasses the HTTP ValidationPipe. Spreading an entire request into Prisma would make future DTO changes easier to turn into accidental privilege changes.

Record<string, unknown> is a TypeScript description of an object with string keys and values that still need checking. Promise<T> describes an asynchronous result. The strategy's record() type predicate performs a runtime object check; each provider field is then validated separately.

blocks.text: The linking migration adds a PostgreSQL check: LOGIN states have no user owner; LINK states must have one. A foreign key connects an owned state to its user and cascades deletion. That check lives in the SQL migration, not as a Prisma field annotation.

Deleting a user cascades images, owned OAuth states, two-factor settings and recovery codes. Refresh tokens and provider records are explicitly deleted first by the service because those relationships do not use that cascade behavior.

blocks.text: Two separate unique fields do not turn into an OR query just by placing both in one where object. If you want 'email already exists OR username already exists', express that OR and use findFirst. A compound unique selector, such as provider_providerUserId, has a different meaning: that pair identifies one row.

An existence check improves the message, but cannot settle a race. Two requests may both see no user and then try to create one. The unique database constraint chooses the winner. Prisma's P2002 error is mapped to HTTP 409. The database, not the early lookup, is the final authority.

select is a data boundary. Requesting only safe fields reduces both transferred data and accidental response leakage. It also clarifies whether a method is returning a public profile, the current user's private account, or an admin view.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: If two simultaneous requests register the same email, where is the race finally stopped? Which methods return a row, which return a list, and which return only a count?

A transaction is a boundary around database work that must succeed or fail together. It is not automatically a lock on the whole database, nor does placing unrelated calls inside one automatically make every race disappear.

rows: The user and initial refresh record are saved together; Discord also creates its provider identity in that nested write.
Consuming the old credential and saving its replacement commit together. A failure rolls the write back.
Repeatable Read gives both queries one database snapshot, keeping a page and its total internally consistent.
The stored bytes and the user's managed URL change together.
A shared advisory lock coordinates rules that span multiple admin users.

blocks.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the selected user row until the transaction ends. Refresh, logout, linking and deletion can coordinate on that same row across multiple service instances. A JavaScript mutex would cover only one process. The SQL is a tagged Prisma template, so interpolated values are parameters rather than SQL text.

Locking only helps operations that take the relevant lock or are blocked by the database's own write locks. The user row is a common coordination point; it is not a magic barrier around every read. Keep network calls and image processing outside these transactions so slow external work does not hold locks.
An important control-flow detail

Refresh-token reuse revokes the session and returns null inside the transaction. That allows revocation to commit. The method throws UnauthorizedException afterward. Throwing inside the callback would roll back the revocation you wanted to preserve.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: A transaction fails while saving the replacement token. Should the original token still work? If you throw immediately after writing a revocation inside the same transaction, does the revocation survive?

Prepare credentials
bcrypt hash, JWT, random refresh secret
blocks.caption: Preparation is not success: registration returns tokens only after the database write succeeds.

blocks.text: Registration checks email or username, hashes the password with bcrypt at cost 12, preallocates a user UUID, and prepares credentials. The nested user.create() stores the password hash and initial refresh row. The role is omitted from user input and defaults to USER. A unique-constraint race becomes 409.

bcrypt is a one-way, salted password hash. Login looks up the exact email and compares the supplied password with bcrypt.compare(). A missing user, an OAuth-only user with no passwordHash, or a wrong password returns the same 'Invalid email or password' message. Equal message text does not prove every failure has identical timing.

A successful login creates a new refresh-session family. It does not reuse the family from another device. The response contains a minimal user object, an access token, a refresh token, Bearer token type, and their lifetimes. Password hashes and provider credentials are excluded.

blocks.text: The password flow creates an active account immediately. emailVerifiedAt remains null, but there is no verification gate or delivery workflow. That is an intentional MVP boundary with an unresolved ownership problem: someone can occupy another person's email before its owner registers.

blocks.text: What is returned if signing succeeds but saving the user fails? Why is bcrypt useful for human passwords while a fast SHA-256 hash can be appropriate for a long random refresh secret?

title: JWTs and your RSA key pair

nodes:
Signature
Proof that signed bytes were not changed
blocks.caption: A compact signed JWT has three base64url segments separated by periods: header.payload.signature.

blocks.text: The header and payload in your access token are encoded, not encrypted. Anyone holding it can decode them. That is expected. Changing the decoded user ID and re-encoding it does not produce a valid signature. Decoding is useful for inspection; verification is required before trusting the contents.

RS256 uses an RSA private key to sign and the matching public key to verify. AuthService calls signAsync({sub: userId}); the JwtModule options supply the private key, algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry. Other services can verify with the public key without gaining the ability to issue valid tokens.

HS256 also signs rather than encrypts. Its difference is that the same shared secret signs and verifies, so every verifier holding that secret can also mint tokens. Encrypted tokens exist as a different construction, but neither your current RS256 token nor an ordinary HS256 JWT hides the payload.

rows: The local user UUID; it is not the Discord user ID.
Expiration / issue time, represented as Unix seconds.
user-service; checks which issuer the verifier accepts.

blocks.text: The generator creates a 3072-bit RSA pair as PEM files under .keys and refuses to overwrite existing files. You copy their contents into .env. PEM is a text representation of a real key, not an arbitrary password string. The public key can be distributed; the private key must stay with trusted signing infrastructure.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: If you can read a token's payload, what is still protected? Why must a verifier check expiry, audience and issuer as well as the signature? How would rotating keys affect still-valid tokens?

AccessTokenGuard extracts a token from Authorization: Bearer ..., calls JwtService.verifyAsync(), and checks that sub is a UUID and exp is numeric. JWT verification also uses the configured RS256 allowlist, issuer, audience and expiry rules. Valid input becomes request.user = {sub}.

A Discord access token cannot be used here: it is a credential for Discord's API. A refresh token cannot be used here either: it has a different format and is checked by the refresh endpoint. Use the accessToken returned by your service.

blocks.text: The access guard does not query a session row. A user deletion does not change an already issued JWT's signature. GET /accounts/me can therefore pass the guard and then return 404 because AccountsService checks the current database. Other services that only verify JWTs need their own account-state policy.

title: The refresh token is not a JWT

blocks.text:
<refresh-record-uuid>.<43-character-random-secret>

const parts = REFRESH_TOKEN_PATTERN.exec(token);
const [, refreshId, secret] = parts;

This is the answer to your earlier regex question. The service is not decoding a JWT here. It deliberately issues an opaque refresh credential consisting of a record ID and a random secret. There is no JSON header or payload to decode. The regex only validates and separates the expected format.

blocks.caption: Knowing the ID alone does not prove possession. The random secret is the credential.

blocks.text: The secret comes from 32 cryptographically random bytes, encoded as 43 base64url characters. Only its SHA-256 hash is stored in the database. A database reader sees the ID and hash, but does not directly obtain the token the client must submit. A raw token leak is different: possession is sufficient to try to use it.

The service computes the submitted hash as bytes, converts the stored hexadecimal hash to bytes, checks equal lengths, then calls timingSafeEqual(). This avoids an ordinary byte-by-byte equality check whose comparison timing can depend on where a mismatch occurs. It does not make the entire endpoint constant-time.
The record has two different identifiers

id identifies one particular refresh credential. sessionId groups all rotations from one login. Refresh changes the ID and secret but carries the sessionId forward. A separate login creates another family. This is why logout can revoke replacements on one device without revoking every device.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: Why do you need both the ID and secret? What information can a database-only attacker recover? What would change if the random secret were replaced with a short human-chosen word?

nodes:
Refresh R1
Revoke R1; create R2 in A

Refresh R2
Revoke R2; create R3 in A
blocks.caption: Login B has its own session family and is not revoked when Session A is revoked.

blocks.text: Refresh first parses the credential, loads its row, verifies the secret hash and checks expiry. Inside a transaction it locks the user row, rereads the token state, prepares a replacement, conditionally revokes the old row and inserts the new one. The client must replace both stored tokens after success.

The conditional update includes the expected ID, hash, unrevoked state and unexpired deadline. Only one request should consume that credential. If saving the replacement or signing fails, the transaction rolls back and the old credential remains usable.
Why a duplicate refresh can log you out

Suppose two browser requests submit R1. The first rotates it to R2. The second waits for the user lock, then sees R1 was already revoked. Because the secret is correct and the token is still within its lifetime, the service treats this as replay and revokes Session A, including R2. The server cannot tell a duplicate client request from a copied token being reused.

The intended client behavior is one in-flight refresh operation that other requests await. React development StrictMode and multiple tabs make this a practical concern, not just an attacker scenario. Your current frontend does not coordinate refresh calls yet.

Each replacement receives another seven-day expiry. There is no absolute session-duration limit, so continued use can extend a session. A replay of an already expired token is rejected before the family-revocation step. Revoked refresh records currently have no scheduled retention cleanup.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: If R2 is returned successfully and immediately fails later, could a second request using R1 explain it? How would you ensure twenty failed API requests trigger only one refresh?

All unrevoked refresh records in that login family are revoked.

blocks.text: Logout accepts the refresh token rather than requiring a current access token. This lets the user log out even when access has expired. A well-formed but unknown token or incorrect secret is silently treated as completed logout; malformed input can still fail DTO validation with 400.

An older rotated token with the correct secret can revoke its family. Logout does not reject merely because that token expired. It acquires the same user lock as refresh, so a replacement created just before logout also belongs to the family being revoked.

Clearing browser storage only removes that browser's local copy. The frontend attempts server logout but currently ignores a network failure. If that request never arrives, the server-side session has not been revoked. Conversely, successful server logout does not erase a copied access token from someone else's machine.

Your decision to accept a short JWT lifetime for the MVP is coherent, but should stay explicit. Immediate rejection in chat/game would require extra state checks or a revocation/account-state mechanism there. The planned MQ layer may distribute that state; it is not implemented by this service today.

That conditional spread was a way to add or omit a property. It was never encryption or asynchronous syntax. The current implementation uses a simple conditional assignment for the email-change rule. The important distinction is absence versus an explicit null.

The public list defaults to page 1 and limit 10. Limits are capped at 100; page must be an integer between 1 and 1,000,000. findMany() retrieves the page while count() counts all matching rows. An empty database reports totalPages 0. A page beyond the last match returns an empty list rather than 404.

Ordering by createdAt descending, then id ascending, gives a deterministic tie-breaker. Repeatable Read keeps the list and total on one snapshot within a response. It does not freeze the dataset across separate page requests. Inserts and deletions between requests can still shift offset-based pages.

A date-only upper bound resolves to midnight; it does not mean 'include that whole calendar day'. Send an explicit timestamp when that distinction matters.

title: Images: from upload to HTTP bytes

blocks.caption: The service validates image content, not merely the filename extension or client-supplied MIME type.

blocks.text: Both routes accept JPEG, PNG and WebP, reject animated/multipage inputs, and cap decoded input at 20 million pixels. Sharp auto-orients, crops with cover positioning, resizes and re-encodes; original metadata is removed by that pipeline. Processing occurs before the database transaction, followed by a processed-size check.

The transaction locks the user, upserts UserImage by (userId, kind), and updates avatarUrl or bannerUrl to the managed relative route. A failure cannot leave a newly committed URL pointing to bytes that were rolled back. Replacing the avatar does not replace the banner.

Public GET image routes return raw bytes through StreamableFile with image/webp, length, inline disposition, no-store and nosniff headers. HTTP supports binary bodies directly; base64 is unnecessary. Another container or a browser can fetch the URL. Relative URLs still need a configured API origin.
Two image sources now exist

Your Discord login update can set avatarUrl to Discord's CDN, including on returning logins. A previous local UserImage row is not deleted, so the blob endpoint may still return an older upload. Linking itself preserves the avatar, but a later Discord login can overwrite its URL. Decide which source should win.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: Why do byte limits not eliminate the need for decoded-pixel limits or rate limits? If a portrait becomes a square avatar, what gets cropped? Would moving bytes to MinIO preserve the profile contract?

nodes:
Admin operation
Validate inputs and enforce mutation rules
blocks.caption: A frontend role badge or hidden button is not an authorization control.

blocks.text: All superadmin routes use both guards in that order. The JWT deliberately does not carry the role. The role guard reads the current database value, so demotion affects the next admin request without waiting for token expiry. Missing accounts yield 401; an authenticated USER receives 403.

The module provides user listing/search, details, creation, profile edits, a separate role-change route, deletion and dashboard counts. Admin creation hashes a password but does not log that user in or create a refresh session. Admin projections include useful profile and role data, never password or token hashes.
Protecting the final superadmin

Admin mutations share a PostgreSQL transaction advisory lock, then recheck the acting user's role inside the transaction. Target-row locks coordinate edits/deletion. A request cannot demote or delete the last SUPERADMIN. This matters under concurrency: two admins must not both count the other as a surviving admin and remove each other.

The bootstrap script promotes an existing account by email and shares the admin advisory lock. It is a trusted local operator command, not a public promotion endpoint. It is idempotent and does not create a user, change its password or issue tokens.

title: Discord login from end to end

blocks.caption: The provider client secret goes from your backend to Discord during the token exchange, not into the browser authorization URL.

blocks.text: DiscordStrategy is an ordinary Nest injectable provider, not a Passport strategy. The controller calls authorize() and authenticate() explicitly. It requests identify/email for login. After checking the callback challenge, it POSTs a form-encoded authorization-code exchange and fetches Discord's /users/@me.

The response is treated as unknown data. The strategy validates the Discord ID, username, token type and other fields before building a smaller profile. global_name falls back to username; email becomes null when absent or invalid; verified is true only for a real boolean true. A validated avatar hash becomes a Discord CDN URL.

AuthService first searches by the stable compound key (DISCORD, providerUserId). A linked identity signs in to its existing local user even if the provider email has changed. An unknown identity needs a valid, verified email to create a user. If that email is already used locally, the request returns 409 and asks the person to use their existing login method.

New-user creation saves User, AuthProvider and initial refresh record together. Local role starts as USER and passwordHash is absent. The service does not retain Discord's access/refresh token; it uses the provider token only to obtain identity. Your application's token pair is issued separately.

Each provider request has a ten-second timeout and rejects redirects. Expected authorization failures map to 401; other upstream failures or malformed responses map to 502. Configuration errors map to 503. Returned messages do not expose provider tokens or raw upstream error bodies.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: Why use the provider ID rather than its username or email as the durable identity? Why must matching email alone never silently connect a provider to an existing local account?

The OAuth state value identifies a short-lived authorization attempt. Your implementation also creates an independent browser secret in an HttpOnly cookie. Hashes of both are stored together. The callback must present the matching state and cookie while the row is unexpired.

rows: Unpredictable challenge values with a constrained wire format.
Bounds how long an unfinished authorization can be completed.
Prevents page JavaScript from reading the cookie directly.
Supports the normal top-level GET navigation back from Discord.
Uses HTTPS cookies for HTTPS callbacks and limits their request path.
Prevents a sign-in challenge being accepted as permission to attach an identity.

blocks.text: The callback reads the stored purpose and owner, then conditionally deletes the row using both hashes, purpose, owner and expiry. The lookup alone authorizes nothing. Only a delete count of one permits continuation. Two concurrent callers cannot both consume the row, even when handled by different service instances.

The cookie is cleared and the challenge is consumed before provider exchange. Denial, timeout or a lost callback response requires starting a fresh attempt. This is a deliberate single-use tradeoff. Expired rows are cleaned when another authorization begins; there is no scheduled cleanup job.

Login and linking use distinct cookies. Starting a second attempt of the same purpose replaces that cookie, so only the latest can finish. localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different cookie hosts. A callback copied to Postman will not automatically carry the browser's secret.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: Why is a valid-looking 43-character state insufficient? Why keep a browser secret separate from the state that appears in the URL? What happens if the callback passes validation but Discord is temporarily unavailable?

title: Linking Discord to an existing user

blocks.caption: This is implemented now. It does not create another local account or issue another token pair.

blocks.text: The start route verifies the access token, locks/rechecks the user, and saves a LINK state with that user ID. The callback does not need a Bearer header because Discord's browser navigation will not carry it. Instead, the matching, single-use browser challenge supplies the previously authenticated owner. A userId body/query parameter cannot redirect the link to someone else.

linkDiscord() locks and rechecks the local user, looks up the external identity, then checks whether that user already has Discord attached. A provider owned by another user returns 409. A different Discord identity already attached to the same user also returns 409. The same identity attached to the same user is an idempotent success after a fresh authorization.

Two database unique constraints back those rules under concurrency. Linking inserts only AuthProvider. It preserves the local email, verification, password, role, username and avatar, and needs only Discord's identify scope. No matching or verified Discord email is required to link: the proof is control of the local account and the provider identity.

Register the second callback URL in Discord's portal. DISCORD_LINK_REDIRECT_URI can override it; otherwise it is /auth/discord/link/callback on the login callback's origin. JSON completion returns provider and providerUserId. HTML completion redirects to AUTH_FRONTEND_URL#providerLinked=discord without issuing tokens.

blocks.label: Questions to carry into the code
blocks.text: What prevents a login callback from being used to link an attacker identity? Why does the callback trust its saved owner instead of an account ID returned by the frontend? What should unlinking require before removing the last login method?

The React/Vite frontend uses VITE_API_URL or http://localhost:3000. Its request helper sends JSON and optionally a Bearer token. A second helper sends image files using FormData and leaves the multipart Content-Type to the browser, which must include the generated boundary.

blocks.caption: The public directory is loaded separately from GET /accounts?page=1&limit=8.

blocks.text: readTokens() restores the saved token object, or reads accessToken and refreshToken from the URL fragment after Discord login. saveTokens() stores them in localStorage. The current backend redirects HTML Discord login callbacks to that fragment; JSON clients still receive the auth response directly.

The profile effect fetches /accounts/me. If that request fails, it attempts refresh, stores the replacement pair and fetches the profile again. signOut() clears the browser state immediately, then attempts server logout with the last refresh token. This gives the UI a simple model but leaves some important coordination issues for the next page.

Profile save is a sequence of separate HTTP requests: PATCH fields, optionally PUT avatar, optionally PUT banner, then GET the refreshed profile. Each request has its own server transaction. A successful profile update is not rolled back if a later banner upload fails.

For linking, the new POST route returns an authorization URL and sets a temporary browser cookie. The frontend must use credentials: 'include', then navigate to that URL. CORS now permits credentials for the configured localhost/127.0.0.1 Vite origins. The current UI has no linking button or completion notification yet; the example in API.md is ready to integrate.

blocks.text: Your intended model gives chat and game local user projections populated by events. They can read their own databases instead of querying the user database for routine display data. That reduces coupling but moves consistency questions into the event contract.

rows: Does chat need displayName and avatarUrl, or also private email and verification data? Include only what the consumer needs.
What happens if the database commit succeeds but publishing fails? An outbox written in the same transaction is one possible answer.
Can the consumer safely process the same event twice? Stable event IDs and idempotent application help.
Can an older profile update overwrite a newer one? A per-user version lets the consumer reject stale updates.
How does a deleted-user event remove projections and cause access to be rejected? What is the expected delay?
Can existing consumers tolerate added fields? Which changes require a new contract version or coordinated rollout?

blocks.text: A 'fat event' should contain only what consumers need. Shipping the full database row would expose unnecessary fields. Apply the same projection discipline used by Prisma select.

Public-key verification answers whether a JWT was issued by a trusted signer and is still within its claims. It does not answer whether an account was deleted five seconds ago. Decide whether a service tolerates the remaining access lifetime, checks current state synchronously, or enforces a local projection updated by events.
Stable user IDs, explicit roles and URL-based media are useful boundaries. Moving image bytes to object storage can preserve avatarUrl/bannerUrl semantics.

blocks.text: Record the request, expected status, actual status, expected database change and observed database change. When your prediction is wrong, locate the exact guard, DTO, service branch or database constraint that explains the result.

1. DTO boundary: forbidden input is rejected before registration writes. Independently, the service never forwards a role from RegisterDto into user creation. Runtime validation and explicit persistence serve different purposes.
2. JWT: decoding does not require a key. Changing signed bytes makes verification fail and yields 401. The public key can verify a signature but cannot generate a valid replacement signature.

3. Sessions: A's old credential identifies the same sessionId as A's replacement. Logout revokes that family. B has a different sessionId and remains refreshable. Already issued access JWTs are a separate lifetime.

4. Replay: one request consumes the original; the next sees a revoked, unexpired credential with a valid secret and revokes the family. A client should coordinate refresh rather than retrying the same credential concurrently.

5. Email: exact equality preserves verification. A changed string clears it. No delivery or verification enforcement follows automatically. Think about case normalization before treating case-only differences as a settled product rule.

6. Pagination: totalPages is 3; the last page has 3 results and the next has none. Your transaction stabilizes one response, not the dataset over multiple requests. Offset movement can repeat or skip a row across pages.
7. Images: two compound keys distinguish AVATAR and BANNER. Upsert replaces the selected kind. The served representation is WebP bytes regardless of a supported original JPEG or PNG upload.

8. Admin: the final admin is protected with 409. A permitted demotion is enforced immediately by the database role lookup on the next request; an old token still identifies the person but no longer grants admin access.

9. Linking: the owned LINK state supplies the local account. The callback adds a provider record without profile changes or new sessions. A later normal Discord login does apply the existing avatar-sync behavior when a provider avatar exists.

10. Callback proof: a valid format, matching email or query user ID is insufficient. Purpose, state, browser secret, owner and expiry must match; the conditional deletion must consume exactly one row.
